title: TSA brings back visitor gate access for some Americans
description: Americans will soon be able to see their loved ones off at airport gates, restoring airport policies that were put in place in the wake of 9/11.The Tr
body: Americans will soon be able to see their loved ones off at airport gates, restoring airport policies that were put in place in the wake of 9/11.The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) announced that it will soon allow individuals without tickets to pass through security and go to airport gates with loved ones.TSA is also considering allowing some US passengers to take full water bottles through security, reversing a policy that was implemented after a foiled 2006 terror plot.The changes represent some of the biggest shifts in aviation security in decades and likely stem from improved technology rather than a decline in standards, an aviation expert told the BBC. Americans who participate in TSA PreCheck or have a known traveller number will be the first to take advantage of the new policies. Those travellers already go through a pre-approval process with the US government in order to receive speedier security screening at US airports. Individuals who have TSA PreCheck and want to go to an airport gate without a ticket can apply online one to three days before their planned visits.TSA announced this week that the Gateside TSA PreCheck programme will be offered at 13 airports across the US. "This new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel," TSA wrote on its website.Jeff Price, an aviation security expert and professor at Metro State University Denver, told the BBC that the post-9/11 policy change was about reducing the number of people security officers had to screen. "It keeps the lines moving and allows us to focus more on the traveling passenger," he said. But now improvements in technology mean these policies can change, he said. In addition to reinstating gate visitors, the Trump administration is also looking at allowing passengers with TSA PreCheck to take water with them through airport security, according to US media reports.That would reverse a ban put in place following attempted terrorist attacks in the UK in 2006, in which individuals planned to smuggle liquid chemical mixtures inside soft drink and sports drink bottles. The BBC requested confirmation of this reported change; TSA did not respond. Price said newer security machines that TSA is installing to replace traditional X-ray machines have computed tomography capabilities, which "can do a much better job of detecting liquid-based explosives".These updates to security protocols follow a move from TSA last year to end the requirement that passengers remove their shoes during security screenings, an unpopular policy in place for two decades.Reaction to the announcements on social media was mixed. Some older users who remember a time before these policies praised a return to normalcy, while younger users questioned whether the changes signaled any decline in safety."People have a nostalgia for a pre 9/11, it's a calling back to a normal world, and I can see that part of it," Price said. "I can see people wanting to get back to something that they feel more comfortable with, which was a pre 9/11 world."But Price said these changes will not impact the safety of passengers as long as core security measures remain in place and standards continue to be high. "I don't want to compromise [valid security measures] simply for a nostalgic feeling before 9/11," he said. "I don't think we should make those types of decisions so that we feel better. We can make those types of decisions as long as the security measures are not compromised, and that's always what I look for in these situations."

schema.headline: TSA brings back visitor gate access for some Americans

title: Four killed and 60 injured in Russian strike on shopping centre, Ukraine says
description: Image source, State Emergency Service of UkraineByPatrick JacksonUkrainian officials say four people were killed and 60 wounded when a Russian drone a
body: Image source, State Emergency Service of UkraineByPatrick JacksonUkrainian officials say four people were killed and 60 wounded when a Russian drone attacked a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, a city in Dnipropetrovsk region.Shops and vehicles were hit in the daylight attack which took place "when the streets were full of people", Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.Two other shopping malls - in the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy - were targeted by Russian air strikes earlier this week, according to Ukrainian media.Russia reported a Ukrainian seaborne drone attack on the resort city of Sochi overnight on Wednesday, in which 28 people were wounded, as well as three more deaths blamed on Ukrainian attacks.A full-scale war has been raging between Russia and Ukraine since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched an invasion more than four and a half years ago.      A new peacemaking effort by envoys sent by US President Donald Trump at the weekend appears to have yielded few concrete results, after talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.   Images released by the State Emergency Service of Ukraine show firefighters directing water hoses at burning vehicles amid clouds of smoke on a street in Pavlohrad.Two of those injured are reported to be members of the service itself, and a child was also hurt.Zelensky offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed in Thursday's attack. "The Russians used drones to kill people who were simply standing near shopping centres," Ukraine's president said in his statement.Pavlohrad, a logistics hub near the central city of Dnipro, has come under heavy attack previously, with two people killed in an attack on warehouses there last month.  Ukrainian officials say a Russian drone attack on a mall in Sumy on Wednesday killed two people and wounded 20. On Thursday, Russian aerial bombing reportedly injured eight people in Sumy, including three children. In Zaporizhzhia, capital of the region of the same name which was partially annexed by Russia soon after the invasion, a shopping mall was almost completely destroyed on Monday, its owners reported.However, it was closed at the time and there were no immediate reports of casualties.  One of the bloodiest attacks on a shopping centre came last month, when Ukrainian officials say Russian drones killed at least 16 people and injured 130 in the city of Kryvyi Rih.  Shopping malls in Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine have also come under attack, with a Ukrainian drone attack reported on Monday on a mall in the port city of Mariupol, Donetsk region, and another attack on the city of Donetsk last month.On Wednesday night, a number of Ukrainian seaborne drones attacked the shoreline at Sochi, Russian officials say. Two of the 28 people reported injured are children.On Thursday, Russian officials reported that a Ukrainian drone strike on the town of Novy Oskol in Belgord Region had killed one person and wounded six others.It was further announced that a Ukrainian attack on a car in Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia on Wednesday had killed a girl of 15, also injuring a child of six and two women; and a separate attack on a civilian lorry in the same region had killed a man.

schema.headline: Four killed and 60 injured in Russian strike on shopping centre, Ukraine says

title: Oil, gas and borrowing costs surge as fears over Middle East escalate
description: The price of oil has jumped to $105 a barrel amid signs the conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved quickly, fuelling fears that inflation co
body: The price of oil has jumped to $105 a barrel amid signs the conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved quickly, fuelling fears that inflation could accelerate. With the conflict between the US and Iran in the Gulf intensifying in recent days, the cost of both crude oil and gas has been rising sharply. Brent crude went back above $100 a barrel on Wednesday and has continued to climb.The war has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, preventing supplies of oil and gas from the Gulf from reaching global markets.US and UK long-term borrowing costs also surged to their highest level in decades.Speaking at a Republican Party convention in Texas on Wednesday, President Trump said he did not think the fighting would end until after the US mid-term elections in November. Analysts said the combination of rising energy costs and higher borrowing costs was adding pressure on financial markets. Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at trading platform IG, said investors were becoming increasingly concerned about the economic impact of higher oil prices. "It feels like investors worldwide are now waking up to the crisis in oil markets," Beauchamp said. He warned that the surge in energy prices could weigh heavily on the global economy if it continues. Concerns have also grown after Iran-aligned Houthi forces were reported to have seized Yemen's port of Mokha, a key Red Sea port.The move could elevate fears of further shipping disruptions.The price of natural gas has also been soaring on wholesale markets. In the UK, it rose above 200p a therm for the first time since the end of 2022.Storage levels in Europe are much lower than normal for the time of year, and the need to fill reserves ahead of the winter has helped to push up prices.

schema.headline: Oil, gas and borrowing costs surge as fears over Middle East escalate

title: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police
description: "These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious mal
body: "These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," the Home Secretary said."This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."The BBC understands that police chiefs are now actively considering using recently-granted powers to completely ban face coverings in specific areas, in light of that demonstration.Saturday's protest was followed 24 hours later with another in which men blocked the only road out of Langstone Harbour, near Portsmouth, after the RNLI had brought ashore 120 migrants.It's unclear at this stage whether further such protests will go ahead - but in some areas of England local groups that have associated themselves with the Patriot Platform umbrella group have called for more demonstrations.The meeting discussed the emergence of Patriot Platform with ministers believing the group aims to intimidate communities.Mahmood is said to have told police chiefs to make better use of intelligence to make sure they had better plans in place ahead of this weekend.That call came after Kent Police had earlier admitted it had been made aware of a potential demonstration in Dover but had not "fully assessed" the warning before the town's nationally critical port road was brought to a standstill.During the meeting, Mahmood is said to have made clear the government expected police to make full use of powers and to deal robustly with any criminal offences.Speaking after the meeting, Deputy Chief Constable Andy Mariner, the National Police Chiefs Council lead for public order, said forces were "continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety".This includes working closely with "local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners" to ensure support is available when needed.He added: "Our priority is to keep people safe, maintain public order and support the right to peaceful and lawful protest. While people are entitled to express their views, anyone committing criminal offences can and should expect police action."Major changes to protest law in the last three years mean officers can now intervene more quickly to end demonstrations that block critical national infrastructure, such as roads to ports.They can also designate an entire area a face mask-free zone for the duration of a protest.It's that second power that police chiefs are now considering using.Police chiefs also say they have initiated an "enhanced and co-ordinated" approach to gathering as much intelligence as possible in the days ahead.

schema.headline: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police

title: Esther Rantzen says she is too fragile to travel to Switzerland to end life
description: Dame Esther Rantzen has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.The veteran br
body: Dame Esther Rantzen has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.The veteran broadcaster, 86, said she would have to fly to the country, where the practice is legal, alone, which she could only have done before her life became "unbearable" and before she was ready to end her life.The Childline founder, who is terminally ill with cancer, first revealed in December 2023 that she had joined the Dignitas clinic.Dame Esther used her statement on Thursday to reiterate a plea for MPs to vote in favour of legalising assisted dying in England and Wales when proposed legislation is revisited by Parliament on Friday.She announced she had joined Dignitas about a year after being diagnosed with stage four lung cancer."Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest," she said."And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process."So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance."Dame Esther added that "everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now", with loved ones either unable to visit her or "see me suffering pain or indignity" when they do.The prominent assisted dying campaigner said the law - which she described as "messy and cruel" - must "change and change quickly".Helping someone end their life is currently considered a criminal offence across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Jersey legalised assisted dying for terminally ill adults earlier this year.MPs are considering a draft law that, if passed, would make it legal in England and Wales under specific circumstances for people who are terminally ill with less than six months to live.While Dame Esther, who is best known for presenting the BBC programme That's Life! for 21 years, is among several leading figures in favour of the bill, there are also campaigners against it, including Paralympian Baroness Grey-ThompsonThey fear that a change in the law could mean that disabled and other vulnerable people could be pressured to end their lives, while also criticising the wording of the proposed legislation as not providing strong enough safeguards.The bill has been through several drafts and has been scrutinised by several Parliamentary committees and the House of Lords, which submitted 1,200 amendments.The bill was previously introduced in 2024, but the last session of Parliament ran out of time before it was passed.It was reintroduced in this Parliament and a second vote will be held on Friday afternoon. If it passes the House of Commons, rarely invoked powers could be used, meaning it would not need the assent of the Lords to become law this time. Proponents of the bill have indicated they would try to bring legislation again as soon as possible were it to be voted down on Friday.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not be voting on the issue and has suggested that palliative and social care should be better funded before legalising assisted suicide is considered.Assisted dying is legal in a number of countries - including Canada, Australia and Belgium - as well as in Switzerland, though the circumstances under which it is legal differ between those nations.

schema.headline: Esther Rantzen says she is too fragile to travel to Switzerland to end life

title: New technology may bring more 9/11 victims' families closure
description: For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life is his mangled firefighter helmet.Scauso's father
body: For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life is his mangled firefighter helmet.Scauso's father, Dennis - part of a New York City Fire Department (FDNY) hazmat unit for 12 years -  initially was not scheduled to work on 11 September, 2001, but switched shifts for the overtime pay.The Long Island father of four was likely in the South Tower of the World Trade Center when it collapsed, the Scauso family was told. The helmet with his badge number was found months later."I've spent essentially my entire life knowing my father died, and learning to live with the fact that we never recovered him," said Scauso, who was four when he died.Dennis Scauso is one of more than 1,000 people killed on September 11 in New York who have yet to be identified, according to New York City's Office of Chief Medical Examiner. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center attacks that day.Last month, the city announced the identity of a previously unknown victim of the terrorist attacks - the 1,654th person - using a new technology called forensic investigative genetic genealogy - or FIGG."There is real promise in using this approach," said Angela Soler, director of forensic anthropology in the city's medical examiner office. "There's hope for more families to receive answers, and hopefully we'll be able to test more remains in the future using this technology as well."Since 9/11, Soler's office has sought to identify the remains of the 2,753 victims who died in the World Trade Center. So far, 60 percent of those killed have been identified."It's been one of the most complex identification efforts that I think anybody has ever really experienced," Soler said.Efforts to identify victims have been complicated by a number of factors.Human remains were damaged in the plane crashes and fires caused by jet fuel, meaning the office had only portions of victims for DNA samples, Soler said.Scauso added that because of the timing of the attacks, many firefighters were changing shifts, but some stayed to help, grabbing whatever extra gear they could find. This meant some first responders recovered were wearing uniforms with others' names, complicating identification.The World Trade Center site also had many more victims than the other 9/11 terrorist attack sites.The remains of five of the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon were never identified because of similar conditions. According to the National Park Service, enough remains were recovered to use DNA, dental records and fingerprints to identify all 40 victims aboard United Airlines flight 93, which crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.Remains from the World Trade Center have been packaged and sealed to help preserve DNA for testing in the years to come. Soon after the attacks, individuals were identified using fingerprints or dental records, but as time went on, when neither was available, the office turned to DNA. Officials were able to use new technology to extract DNA and retest the same remains."That's why all these years down the road, we're still getting new identifications, because we're just continuing to retest and retry with every new technology that becomes available," Soler said.DNA technology has helped the office identify 1,495 victims since 9/11 - some solely with DNA and others with multiple methods - according to the medical examiner's office.Last year, the city announced that with the help of DNA, 24 years later, it had identified three new victims - Ryan Fitzgerald, a 26-year-old currency trader, Babara Keating, a 72-year-old who was aboard American Airlines Flight 11 from Boston to Los Angeles, and a woman whose family kept her identity private.Soler said the new FIGG technology uses whole genome sequencing - which provides a way to read someone's entire genetic code. It means investigators can make more potential matches to family members who are more distant relatives of the victim. Once those matches are made, the New York Police Department helps find relatives who are closer to the victims.The medical examiner's office in New York still gets weekly calls from loved ones asking about someone whose remains were never recovered.Many have never been able to bury a loved one, but some families choose to leave the remains - once found - at a repository at the 9/11 memorial site in New York. The repository was built into the bedrock of the World Trade Center site and can only be accessed by medical examiner staff. A nearby private space, known as the reflection room, is available for families to mourn."That's where their loved one was in their last moments, and that's where they want them to stay", Soler said.Some don't want to be notified, perhaps because the confirmation is too painful, said Soler, who helps inform families.Scauso is one of those people. She knows people who, in recent years, got a call that a relative finally has been identified. The thought of being next on the list is scary for her family, who has worked hard to keep the memory of her father - a jack of all trades and a lover of jazz - alive."At this point, an identification wouldn't change the reality of his death. It wouldn't give me back my father, and I don't necessarily want to reopen something that has become part of the way I've learned to live and grieve," she said. "Especially 25 years later, it's going to open up the wounds again."But, Scauso said, the technology is important.Soler has seen the news provide a mix of both relief and sadness. "It's confirmation of something that they always knew to be true - they knew their loved one died on 9/11, but I think for many families, there's still that question in the back of their mind until the remains are formally identified," Soler said."Maybe they're reliving it a little bit more now, having this new identification. But at the same time, it closes one chapter of their journey after 9/11," she added.To Soler - and some of her current colleagues who also were on the ground during 9/11 - the work is deeply personal. Workers from their office arrived at Ground Zero after the planes hit the towers, and were there when the buildings collapsed.They are aware it is unlikely they will identify every victim of the New York attacks. In some instances, there may be no remains of a victim at all. Still, they have no plans to stop."As long as there's families looking for answers, we'll continue searching for them," she said.

schema.headline: New technology may bring more 9/11 victims' families closure

title: Yemen's Houthis reportedly seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha
description: Yemen's Houthis have seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, military sources and witnesses say.Mokha
body: Yemen's Houthis have seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, military sources and witnesses say.Mokha's capture leaves the Iran-backed group only 75km (46 miles) away from the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a trade route that links Asia and Europe.The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.Mokha residents said Houthi fighters moved into the city after fierce clashes with pro-government forces on Wednesday night, prompting many families to flee their homes."The takeover came without warning. Panic spread throughout the area, forcing people to flee amid distressing scenes of injured people lying in the streets with no-one there to help them," one man told BBC Arabic's Middle East Lifeline programme.Another man said that Houthi fighters were patrolling the streets of Mokha on Thursday, while government offices and shops were closed."At the moment, we don't know what Ansar Allah will do," he added, using the group's formal name. "Everyone is afraid for their safety."Many displaced families are heading east towards the city of Aden, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based."We fled with our children and kept running. We have no bedding, no home, nothing with us. Everything was destroyed within an hour. They didn't even give us a chance or warn us beforehand," one woman told BBC Arabic."We are women with no means of defending ourselves, and we have innocent children with us."There was no immediate confirmation of Mokha's capture from the Houthis.But the group's Supreme Political Council said in a statement on Thursday that clashes had "ceased in the western coast districts after the expulsion of Saudi enemy mobilisations", according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.Tarek Salah, leader of the pro-government National Resistance Forces, also said he had moved his command centre on the west coast to a "safe location".He added that his forces had paid "a heavy price in recent days in the face of a Houthi offensive that was planned and supported by Iran".A Yemeni military source told AFP news agency that Houthi fighters had also seized Zuqar Island in the Red Sea, about 80km north-west of Mokha, after launching a barrage of rockets and a ground assault using boats.Meanwhile, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, urged Arab states and other countries to help protect Yemen's coasts and restore state control.The Houthis' Supreme Political Council asserted its "right to defend [Yemen's] sovereignty and territorial waters while simultaneously reassuring the international community that navigation in the Red Sea remains safe".However, the Houthi-run humanitarian operations co-ordination centre also stressed that the embargo on Saudi ships remained in place.Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said Saudi warplanes carried out 64 strikes across the western provinces of Taiz, Hudaydah, Marib and Jawf over the previous 24 hours.There was no immediate comment from the Saudi military.However, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday evening that it would respond to a series of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the south-western Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan.On Tuesday, the Houthis launched dozens of drones and missiles at southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 civilians and causing fires at several oil facilities that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi authorities.The Houthis said they were retaliating for dozens of Saudi air strikes on territory they control in recent days, including one on a prison in the town of Hazm in Jawf province on Monday that they said killed at least 23 civilians.The Saudi-led coalition has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Yemen's Houthis reportedly seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha

title: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
description: Image source, EPAByAlex BoydUS President Donald Trump has offered every adult American $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win November's midterm elections
body: Image source, EPAByAlex BoydUS President Donald Trump has offered every adult American $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win November's midterm elections, but it is unclear how such a plan would be funded and whether it is legal.His remarks prompted raucous applause from supporters at a party convention on Wednesday night, although Democrats labelled it an "empty promise".Trump also told the Republican conference that the money would have to be spent in the US, but it is unclear how that would be monitored.US Vice-President JD Vance suggested it might be paid for by tariff revenue and that such cheques would not go to wealthy Americans. Is Trump's offer legal?Under US federal law, it is illegal to give payments that are intended to influence the way a person is voting.However, some experts have said the offer made by Trump in Texas on Wednesday could be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal.Dr Joan Mahoney, lecturer in law at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she thought the offer would be legal, though she said politicians "don't usually do it quite this explicitly"."On the one hand it sounds a bit like a bribe, vote for the Republicans and you'll get money, which would be decidedly illegal," she said."But on the other hand it would go to everyone, regardless of how they voted so it isn't in that sense a bribe."I think it would be legal. It's the same kind of campaign pledge as saying 'if my party wins we'll reduce taxes'. Every party does that all the time... and that's obviously perfectly legal."However, Laurel Rapp, director of the US and North America programme at Chatham House, told the BBC that Trump's offer seemed to be "a very different, very transactional agreement" from the kind of promise usually made by candidates in an election period.Figure caption, Watch: BBC North America editor Sarah Smith looks into whether Trump's promise stands upHow much would it cost?Aside from the question of legality, some have also asked whether Trump's offer would be feasible financially in the context of increasing US debt, partially as a result of the war in Iran.There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.Trump gave no details on how such cheques would be funded.Congress authorises spending in the US, but the president did not say whether he planned to ask for legislative approval for any payments. And legal experts said it was unlikely he could approve such a vast sum via a presidential executive order.Erica York, a senior economist at the Washington DC-based Tax Foundation, told the BBC she would be "extremely surprised" if Congress approved any proposal."This would be one of the worst ways to use $1.3 trillion," she said. "We're on a very unsustainable track, with deficits only projected to grow and grow," York added. Could tariff revenue fund it?Speaking to Fox News after Trump's speech, Vice-President Vance indicated that the payments could be funded by money raised by the president from tariffs.However, such revenue to date falls far short of the money that would be needed to account for Trump's $5,000 cheques offer.According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the US has brought in around $475bn in tariff and excise tax revenue since the beginning of 2025. But more than $100bn has been refunded after the Supreme Court struck down many tariffs earlier this year.When asked how the payouts could work, the White House said in a statement to the BBC: "The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump.""With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results," added spokesman Davis Ingle.Why has Trump made the offer?One former Republican strategist and pollster said Trump's latest offer should be firmly seen in the context of an election that is now less than two months away. "It is an extraordinary promise, and I'm not sure where that money is going to come from - but it is campaign season," Robert Moran told the BBC.Chatham House's Rapp said Trump was thinking short term to try to keep hold of Congress as he enters the final two years of his term in office."Money is something that he is now resorting to because the polling is not looking good for Republicans and the polling is not looking good for him," she continued.Has anything similar happened before?Trump has previously proposed $2,000 cheques to be funded by tariff revenues, but those payouts have not materialised.Former President Joe Biden was accused of buying votes when he promised $2,000 Covid stimulus cheques for Americans if Democrats won Senate elections in Georgia in January 2021.A similar controversy arose ahead of the 2024 presidential election, during which billionaire Trump supporter Elon Musk offered cash incentives to registered voters in seven swing states who signed a certain petition.Additional reporting by Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter

schema.headline: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?

title: England vs Pakistan: Brook, Smith, Lawrence and Robinson push hosts towards third Test win
description: Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day two of five)Pakistan 133 (Shakeel 43; Tongue 4-42) & 52-2 (Robinson 2-10)England 453 (Brook 75, Smith 69, Lawrence
body: Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day two of five)Pakistan 133 (Shakeel 43; Tongue 4-42) & 52-2 (Robinson 2-10)England 453 (Brook 75, Smith 69, Lawrence 65, Gay 60, Robinson 50; Razaullah 4-148)Pakistan are 268 runs behindScorecardEngland's charge towards a two-day win in the final Test against Pakistan was only halted by rain at Edgbaston.The tourists were battling for survival on 52-2 - 268 adrift of making England bat again - when the bad weather intervened for a second and final occasion in Birmingham.The time was 17:07 BST. With the possibility of an extra half an hour available to force a result, play could have continued until 19:00 if conditions had allowed.Given the fragility of the Pakistan batting - the tourists have not reached 200 or batted for more than 51 overs in the series - there was a real possibility England would earn victory inside two days after Ollie Robinson reduced the visitors to 0-2.Instead, the players will return on Friday, when England will complete a 3-0 series clean sweep.The eventual outcome of this match was barely in doubt when England began Thursday on 156-4, leading by 23.Contributions of 75 from Harry Brook, 69 by Jamie Smith, 65 scored by Dan Lawrence and 50 from Robinson pushed England to 453, a huge first-innings lead of 320.The only disappointment was that no England batter pushed on to make a century, meaning Ben Duckett's ton against New Zealand at Trent Bridge will remain the home side's only hundred of the summer.One of the criticisms of the previous England regime, under captain Ben Stokes and coach Brendon McCullum, was their inability to finish series strongly.England have lost the final Test in each of their past six series. Some of their worst performances in the Bazball era came in dead rubbers after a series had been won, notably at home to Sri Lanka in 2024 and away to New Zealand later the same year.Stokes often said he did not like the word "ruthless" and there were plenty of times his side lacked ruthlessness. On this occasion, Root's England are showing their ruthless side.The quality of the opposition should be taken into account - Stokes' England would have comfortably beaten this poor Pakistan side. The hosts also had the better of the conditions on Thursday, batting under blue sky then bowling when it got dark overhead.But, under Root, England are showing a new-found calmness, along with a willingness to find the right tempo to their batting. The way they extended their lead on the second day was an example of a more mature approach.And, in Robinson, they have a bowler in the form of his life, a purple patch England will hope carries through the winter and to next summer's Ashes.Given England's dominance over Pakistan, it is curious that none of their batters have registered a century in the series and now will not get another chance.Duckett's sole ton means England will end a six-Test home summer with their fewest number of individual hundreds.Brook, Lawrence and Smith all impressed, and all will be disappointed they missed out on three figures.A stand of 86 between Brook and Lawrence was full of intent at the beginning of the day, with Lawrence the aggressor. Busy running was a feature of the stand, until Brook attempted a needless single to mid-wicket and was run out at the non-striker's end.Lawrence has made three half-centuries since being recalled at the beginning of this series, probably enough to earn a place in South Africa in December. This is his 17th Test and he gave an audible cry of frustration when he chopped on off Mohammad Imran, extending a wait for a maiden hundred.Smith suffered a tough Ashes tour, yet has shown signs of rehabilitation with bat and wicketkeeping gloves this summer. On a ground where he has had plenty of previous success, he muscled the ball through the leg side before he offered a tame return catch to Razaullah.Robinson can do no wrong at the moment. He swiped through the leg side, including a massive six into the Hollies Stand, for his second half-century in Test cricket. Robinson's previous 50 came against India in Ranchi in 2024, his last before being dropped. Now he is indispensable.Even Jofra Archer got involved, heaving two sixes of his own. He was left unbeaten on 32 when last man Josh Tongue was caught behind.

schema.headline: England vs Pakistan: Brook, Smith, Lawrence and Robinson push hosts towards third Test win

title: England rugby union: Captain Meg Jones calls for fertility support
description: Meg Jones, captain of England women's rugby union team, wants Red Roses players to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.Speaking to BBC S
body: Meg Jones, captain of England women's rugby union team, wants Red Roses players to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.Speaking to BBC Sport, Jones said: "Why should my opportunity to have a family be taken away from me because I want to pursue my career?"Jones revealed she has already started her fertility journey with her fiancee after visiting a clinic to have their egg count checked.The 29-year-old says that she's an "open book" on some subjects and wants to "share her journey" as she discusses both her upcoming wedding and family planning with equal comfort."We were looking to freeze, but actually the advice was we don't need to freeze yet so we can probably wait till after the wedding," said Jones. "That's where we were going to look to conceive."The Red Roses are considered to have one of the best maternity policies in international women's sport, with two World Cup winners having recently given birth and two more expecting.When approached about providing fertility packages for England players, a Rugby Football Union (RFU) spokesperson said: "We work hard to support players in the decisions they make around fertility and family planning and are proud to have been at the forefront of industry-leading support in this area."We already have comprehensive maternity and parental policies in place and are always open to exploring how that support can evolve."While there is no specific policy around financial compensation for fertility treatment for England players, it is understood there are ongoing discussions at the RFU and it could be introduced in the future.Players are currently entitled to a week of paid leave per treatment cycle for treatment and appointments.Jones first said that the Red Roses should "jump on that" policy while on the  on "The Good, The Scaz & The Rugby" podcast when discussing the Spanish football federation's announcement, external that it would pay for its international women's players to freeze their eggsIn August, Chelsea Women also unveiled a partnership, external with a fertility company to provide workshops, treatments, counselling and assessments to support their players.It was revealed in The Observer, external that the fund set up by Chelsea would cover the cost of the whole squad freezing their eggs.Speaking before England's match with Australia on Saturday Jones told BBC Sport: "I wouldn't have thought it was something that we were lacking from maybe a governing point of view, but now I think about it I'm like, yeah, actually, I haven't got that opportunity to go and create a family and be guided on."It's definitely been flagged with our group. And yeah, again, you learn so much from other teams… And I think the more we can empower women the better for the game as a whole, and better for women in general."

schema.headline: England rugby union: Captain Meg Jones calls for fertility support

title: Middlesbrough dad charged with A66 crash funeral assault
description: The father of one of the five men who were killed in a wrong-way crash with a police car has been charged with assaulting someone at his son's funeral
body: The father of one of the five men who were killed in a wrong-way crash with a police car has been charged with assaulting someone at his son's funeral.Gye Worthy, 39, was arrested at Teesside Crematorium in Middlesbrough following a disturbance during the service on Wednesday.His son Cole Worthy, 17, died when the Volkswagon Passat he and four others were in collided with a marked armed police car on the A66 in South Bank in the early hours of 22 August.Cleveland Police said Gye Worthy has been charged with common assault and obstructing police and  is due to appear at Teesside Magistrates' Court in October.Cole Worthy's funeral was held on the same day as that of PC Matthew Blades, 37, who was one of the officers killed in the crash.PC Blades had been travelling along the A66 with his colleague PC Tom Clough when their car was struck head-on by the Passat travelling in the wrong direction.The pair were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered a camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit which preceded the crash, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

schema.headline: Middlesbrough dad charged with A66 crash funeral assault

title: We Will Rock You theatregoer who attacked singing woman is jailed
description: Prosecutor Sam Lubner said Potier had been at the show, which is based on the music of the rock band Queen, with his theatre critic partner Lizzie Lov
body: Prosecutor Sam Lubner said Potier had been at the show, which is based on the music of the rock band Queen, with his theatre critic partner Lizzie Loveridge.He said O'Donnell and a friend had started singing, then Loveridge - using a profanity - told them to "shut up".O'Donnell suggested the reaction was "rude", but Potier responded by saying "I'll show you what rude is" before attacking her.The court was told the attack lasted a few seconds.Potier and Loveridge were later tracked down thanks to the business card she had given out to O'Donnell, and he was arrested in November 2023.O'Donnell was not physically injured, but she told the judge she was "more wary" of her surroundings since the attack and "far more conscious" of her "physical safety"."I want to set an example for the young women and girls in my life, that this sort of behaviour is not acceptable," she said.She also described hearing Potier "laughing" outside court during the trial, talking about his belief that he would not be given a prison sentence partly because of his age.The judge was told how Potier was given a six-year jail sentence in 2002 for inciting the murder of his former partner in Australia.He was given a further 12-year sentence in 2006 for trying to arrange her murder again.Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.

title: Labour mayors in England vow to cap tourist tax at 5%
description: Labour's regional mayors in England have pledged to cap a new fee on visitors' overnight stays at 5%, after hospitality bosses warned it could put job
body: Labour's regional mayors in England have pledged to cap a new fee on visitors' overnight stays at 5%, after hospitality bosses warned it could put jobs at risk. Local leaders are set to gain new powers to charge an uncapped levy, dubbed a "tourist tax", as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.But the Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge if they do apply it, adding that they had listened to concerns over costs.Reform UK's two regional mayors and the two Conservative ones are likely to oppose any levy given criticism from their national parties of the policy.In a letter to Chancellor John Healey and Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner, the Labour metro mayors said 5% represented a "reasonable ceiling" on the tax."It provides a balance of ensuring that local levies are not excessive, or vary significantly between regions, while also leaving room for local variation as appropriate," they added.They added this would still allow for "meaningful investment" in local areas, whilst stressing any future levies in their areas would be "subject to local consultation".The letter was signed by Labour mayors in London, Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, West Midlands, North East, West of England, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, East Midlands and York and North Yorkshire.The government had earlier pledged to protect budget holidays "by making sure low-cost accommodation always pays lowest levy" and said the extra cash could be invested in high streets and local transport.While Labour mayors have backed the new levy, others have expressed caution or signalled they will not bring it in.Local leaders, including heads of Foundation Strategic Authorities where there is no mayor, will need to clarify by early 2028 how the revenue raised should be reinvested.They will also be allowed to offer exemptions, such as for campsites. However, mayors will not be allowed to exempt whole localities within their regions from the tax, to avoid creating confusion for visitors and businesses.The government said it would introduce a bill to Parliament "in due course" to bring in the levy, which would apply to both Britons and people visiting from abroad.Leading trade body UKHospitality has hit back, saying the levy means "jobs are now at risk".Its chief executive Allen Simpson claimed it would add about £100 to £120 on average to the cost of a family holiday in England, amid fears mayors would make use of the fact there is, in theory, no upper limit for the levy. "We know, don't we, that local government is struggling for funds - it was hit very hard by austerity," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme."If you only devolve one tax raising power, of course local mayors are going to pull that lever until it snaps."He added: "It will be the case that you'll have holiday parks which can't open in the shoulder seasons [between peak and low season] and of course people who go on holiday will just have that little bit less money in their pocket."Conservative shadow housing secretary David Simmonds said: "VAT is already charged at 20% on hotels - much higher than in other countries - and now they'll pay VAT on this tourism tax too: a Labour double whammy."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said his party's two mayors in Greater Lincolnshire and Hull and East Yorkshire "won't touch" the levy, which he described as a "holiday tax".The idea was first raised under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in November and is similar to schemes running in Scotland and European destinations.Two cities in England already run their own voluntary schemes - a £1 per room, per night City Visitor Charge in Manchester, introduced when Burnham was mayor of the region, and a £2 nightly charge in Liverpool. These are business-led schemes where hotels choose to pool the money raised to support local tourism.Until now, regional mayors have not had the power to bring such fees in themselves - but they argue it is needed to boost economic growth.Conservative Mayor of Tees Valley Ben Houchen ruled out, external introducing any tourist tax last year.John Chappell, who runs five caravan parks in Skegness, Lincolnshire, told BBC Your Voice that many English tourist resorts have visitors on tight budgets already struggling with the cost of car travel. He said an extra cost would "kill the industry off". "Tourists are the saviours of our resorts, not the demons and ill thought-out ideas like these show how out of touch with reality politicians are," he added.The taxes are common in Europe and the rest of the world, with New York, Amsterdam and Rome applying overnight charges to accommodation stays to fund local services. However, they are capped in several European cities.In Scotland local authorities can charge a visitor levy on overnight accommodation. In Edinburgh, the rate is 5% for those staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering facilities - capped at five nights.It has had a mixed reaction, with some praising extra investment but Scottish Ballet responded by cutting performances while criticising the "unsustainable economics of touring in Edinburgh".In Wales, a capped levy of £1.30 per person per night is set to be introduced in April next year, but it will be up to local authorities to decide whether to roll it out.

schema.headline: Labour mayors in England vow to cap tourist tax at 5%

title: Spanish Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton says he and Charles Leclerc have 'squashed' Monza controversy
description: Lewis Hamilton says he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc have "squashed" any controversy between them after a difficult Italian Grand Prix.Leclerc
body: Lewis Hamilton says he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc have "squashed" any controversy between them after a difficult Italian Grand Prix.Leclerc forced Hamilton into the gravel at the first chicane at Monza on Sunday, and then crashed two laps later. Hamilton recovered to finish a disappointed sixth.It was the second flashpoint between the Ferrari drivers in two races, after an argument over the radio during the Dutch Grand Prix when Leclerc resisted a request to move aside for Hamilton.Hamilton said: "What's great is that there was no shying away from having a discussion. We sat face to face, just him and I, and talked about it."We were just both open and honest, and we squashed it. We can move on. I think that one shows the maturity from him."Speaking at the media day for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, the seven-time champion added: "It's healthy. It's a relationship we have built over time. Of course, there's going to be frustrations and I'm sure there'll be more times where we're close because we're very close in pace."We both want to win just as much as each other, and we both want to do well for the team as well."Leclerc said: "It's kind of clear that we never want to see a car of the same team in the grass."After reviewing, we spoke with Lewis. I obviously know I went too far in turn two and I said it to Lewis and I think it's very clear what we should do or should avoid going forward."But I won't go into much more details of what we've said. The only thing I can say is that it definitely did not affect the good relationship that we have and it will not affect anything going forward. And that is the most important for me, really."I know we are driving for Ferrari and if there's one race where you don't want that to happen, it's in Monza and when these things happen at our home race, then it does a huge mess outside."However, looking at the race from outside, there's been also some friction between other team-mates and the only thing we end up speaking of is Lewis and me, which I don't think is quite right. But that doesn't mean we did everything perfect."Hamilton acknowledged again that Ferrari had to improve their operations, after three consecutive race weekends where qualifying has not gone to plan."It's really just making sure we're executing to make sure we get the best result for the team," he said. "Instead of us working against each other and finish fourth and fifth, maybe we can work together and get a podium and pull off more points."It's a longer term process. It's not something we can just change into this weekend. There's a huge amount of moving parts, there's a lot of people, there's a culture that's been there for a long, long time and moving big pieces is not so easy."F1 faces a fresh challenge this weekend at the first Spanish Grand at the new Madring, a hybrid street circuit built on the Ifema complex near the city's international airport.Hamilton said: "It's a massively challenging circuit. Of all the new tracks that I've gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, are the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines and such."Mercedes driver George Russell said: "It's a crazy circuit, I would put it. Arguably one of the most risky circuits of the whole calendar."Because you have real high-speed corners, sort of Jeddah-esque, the walls are very close, so there's no margin for error, but then you have other corners... where you're coming from a high speed into a slow braking zone, you're braking and turning at the same time, so locking tyres are going to be easy and if you lock up you'll be straight in the wall."So, excited to try that out, I think it's going to be really challenging for us as drivers, the race is going to be challenging to overtake, so on the whole it's not an easy one."Russell heads into the race 66 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli after the Italian's landmark victory in Monza from 19th on the grid.The Briton acknowledged that his title hopes with nine or 10 races left, amid uncertainty about the end of the season, were fading fast."I would definitely need some luck and I need some good performances," Russell said. "It's not really something I'm thinking about, because he's performing better than me, so he deserves to be leading the championship."There's still a long way to go, but he's yet to have a bad weekend in terms of performance."So he's performing exceptionally well, my performances are better, but if I want to win this championship, I'm going to need some luck on the way. But it's not something I'm focused on. I'm focused on driving faster and just finding more performance."Antonelli said: "I don't really want to try thinking about the championship. I think Monza was the proof that I wasn't driving thinking about, or worrying about the championship. I was just driving to win, to do my best. So that's the mindset."The Italian said his win in Monza was "so far the best day of my life and definitely one I will remember forever".He said a day karting with Mercedes on Monday helped him move on from the excitement of the day before."After Monza, that night, that day overall, I was very excited. But then going karting on Monday helped me to go back to earth, just go back to the ground."It was a good day, good fun day with the team. It was also a way to remind myself where I came from, all the journey that was done."And then about pressure, I try to embrace it as much as possible. And I try to see it as a positive thing and try to see it as an opportunity too. That's also what is helping me to stay calm under difficult situations."

schema.headline: Spanish Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton says he and Charles Leclerc have 'squashed' Monza controversy

title: 'My cancer spread while I waited 128 days for an op':  The cost of England's care gap
description: Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up w
body: Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex."I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan.On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery.Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe.Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2029.But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better.Now, 71.2% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%.Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 2,800 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target.That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type.Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time".  For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%, on average.By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist.He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan.Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal.One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets.  Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity.Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country.But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin.Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers."We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can."Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, Bolton NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part.Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement."If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan for England, it must match ambition with urgency," said Steve Haines of Macmillan Cancer Support.He said that "visible progress" was needed on a promise to set up a National Cancer Board to oversee progress on improving waiting times and treatment.A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson says "cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction will all three cancer standards better than a year ago".They concede that "there is more to do," and that the plan "will help people get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner."Additional reporting Daniel Wainwright and Jess Carr

schema.headline: 'My cancer spread while I waited 128 days for an op':  The cost of England's care gap
